name: Valley Cell Simplification
text:
# Valley Cell Simplification

Also called: Persistence-based topological simplification

## Overview
Valley Cell Simplification is a topological noise reduction method that removes insignificant "valley cells" from a [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) of a scalar field (typically a 2D density plot for transfer function design) by merging adjacent cells based on boundary persistence [S1]. It solves the problem of over-segmentation caused by noise, where small, semantically irrelevant features fragment the data space [S1]. Unlike standard watershed transformations which produce a flat partition, this method operates hierarchically, allowing the user to control the level of detail via a persistence threshold, effectively filtering out noise while preserving significant peaks [S1].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:**
- Input: A set of valley cells $C = \{c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n\}$ forming a partition of the domain, and the boundary persistence value $P(b)$ for every boundary $b$ separating two adjacent cells [S1].
- Output: A simplified set of valley cells $C'$ where cells with boundary persistence below a threshold $\tau$ have been merged [S1].

**Data Structures:**
- **Cell:** Contains a set of local maxima associated with the cell [S1].
- **Boundary:** Connects two adjacent cells. Stores the persistence value $P$ [S1].
- **Priority Queue:** Stores all boundaries, ordered by ascending persistence value [G].

**Pseudocode:**
> **Unverified code.** The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors.

```python
def valley_cell_simplification(cells, boundaries, threshold):
    # cells: dict mapping cell_id -> set of local_maxima
    # boundaries: list of (id, cell_a, cell_b, persistence)
    # threshold: float, max persistence to merge
    pq = MinPriorityQueue(boundaries, key=lambda b: b.persistence)
    active_cells = set(cells.keys())
    
    while pq and pq.min_key <= threshold:
        b = pq.pop()
        if b.cell_a not in active_cells or b.cell_b not in active_cells:
            continue
        c_new = merge_adjacent_cells(b.cell_a, b.cell_b, cells)
        active_cells.add(c_new)
        active_cells.discard(b.cell_a)
        active_cells.discard(b.cell_b)
        
        old_boundaries = [bnd for bnd in boundaries if bnd.cell_a in (b.cell_a, b.cell_b) or bnd.cell_b in (b.cell_a, b.cell_b) if bnd != b]
        for bnd in old_boundaries:
            pq.remove(bnd)
            
        new_boundaries = compute_new_boundaries(c_new, active_cells, cells)
        for nb in new_boundaries:
            pq.push(nb)
            
    return {cid: cells[cid] for cid in active_cells}
```

**Parameters:**
- **Persistence Threshold ($\tau$):** The cutoff for merging [S1]. Typical values range from $0.1\%$ to $1.5\%$ of the maximal persistence value observed in the dataset [S1].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
- **Precision:** Persistence values can be very small. Floating-point precision errors may affect the ordering in the priority queue [G].
- **Degenerate Input:** If the density plot has no significant peaks, all cells may be merged into one [S1]. The algorithm should handle the case where the queue empties before reaching the threshold [G].

## Subtopics

### Valley Cell Hierarchy Construction
This variant constructs a tree structure representing the hierarchy of features by reversing the simplification process [S1]. It starts with the simplified valley cells and merges them in order of increasing boundary persistence [S1]. When two cells are merged, parent-child relationships are established, and the maximum sets and boundary persistences of remaining boundaries are updated [S1]. The root of the resulting tree corresponds to the cell containing the largest local maximum [S1]. This hierarchy allows for interactive merging and splitting of features [S1].

## Operating characteristics
- **Time Complexity:** Dominated by the sorting of boundaries and the priority queue operations [G]. If $N$ is the number of boundaries, the complexity is approximately $O(N \log N)$ for initialization and $O(N \log N)$ for the merging process, assuming constant-time updates to boundary properties [G].
- **Memory Complexity:** Linear in the number of cells and boundaries, $O(N)$, to store the cell maxima sets and boundary persistence values [G].
- **Performance:** The method is efficient for 2D density plots [S1]. The sources note that a high percentage of persistence values are very small, meaning many merges occur quickly at low thresholds [S1].
- **Strengths:** Automatically generates meaningful clusters without requiring manual bin size selection (unlike frequency binning) [S1]. It provides a hierarchical view of the data, allowing users to explore features at different scales [S1].
- **Limitations:** The quality of the simplification depends heavily on the correct estimation of boundary persistence [S1]. If the persistence metric does not accurately reflect the separability of peaks, noise may be retained or significant features may be merged [S1].

## Background
The method was introduced by Y. Wang et al. in the paper "Automating Transfer Function Design with Valley Cell-Based Clustering of 2D Density Plots" (2012) [S1]. It is based on Morse complex theory and is described as a hierarchical variant of the watershed transformation [S1]. The concept of using persistence to measure the significance of topological features (specifically saddle-maximum pairs) originates from earlier work by Edelsbrunner, Harer, and Zomorodian [S1]. The authors observed that 10% of maximal persistence is sufficient to remove insignificant features in general volume data [S1]. They adapted the threshold range to $0.1\% - 1.5\%$ specifically for 2D density plots [S1].
